8 KNOTS

Knots turn up three ways: pale and dull in a supermarket basket; blistered and salty
from a pizzeria oven; o, if your neighbor is generous, warm and dripping and gone %
before anyone has sat down.

DOUGH

2Y% cups (300g) stone-ground all-
purpose flour
%: teaspoon salt

1 teaspoon sugar

2. teaspoons instant yeast
"to 1 cup (196g to 224g) water, warm*

TOPPING

"a cup (112g) water, warm

1 teaspoon sugar

flaky sea salt (optional)
3 tablespoons (42g) salted butter,
melted

Place the flour, salt, sugar, yeast and water into a bowl and stir into a shaggy mass. Work
the dough for about 6 minutes, by machine or on the counter, until it feels supple and
slightly tacky. Scrape it into an oiled bowl, cover, and leave it alone for 30 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 450°F. Set out two sheet pans and rub them with a little
olive oil or lay a square of baking paper on each.

Turn the dough onto an oiled counter and cut it into 8 even portions
(roughly 64g apiece). Give the portions a short rest, uncovered, for § minutes.

Stretch every portion into a rope (around 12") and tie it loosely into
a knot (the drawing on page 204 helps), Dunk the knots in the warm sugared water
and set them on the pans. Scatter over the sea salt, if you like.
Give them 10 minutes, uncovered, while the oven comes up.

VARIATION

HERB STICKS: For long skinny sticks, follow the dough as far as its first rest.
Cut it into 24 portions and roll each one out to a 9” to
10” stick. Lay the sticks on an oiled pan, paint them with a little water, and press
over chopped rosemary. Rest and bake them just as you would the knots above.

KEEP IT!

Plain lean doughs keep beautifully in the fridge or the freezer for a short while. The ones that
sulk are rich doughs, which carry on working after a day or two in the cold (the
freezer suits them better); or doughs with wet things folded in,
such as olives, cheese, or roasted peppers. Those weep as they
come back to room temperature.
Our habit is to mix the dough, give it one rise, knock it back, and freeze it flat before it can
come up again. For a loaf, we shape the
_ dough, drop it in a greased tin, slide the tin into a plastic bag, tie it, and freeze for
3 24 hours; after that the dough comes out of the tin and goes back,
double-wrapped, into the
freezer.
On baking day, unwrap the dough, return it to its greased tin, lay
oiled film over it, and leave it on the counter. Figure on 4 hours for it to wake up
and start moving, and anot
her hour before it fills the tin;

a warm room will shorten that a good deal. You also may thaw

the dough in the tin in the refri
gerator overnight, then give it

its last rise in the morning.
For best results, frozen dough ought to be used within 2to 3 Le
before it starts to lose its lift.
